This method transforms the ray into the ellipsoid's local space, solves a quadratic equation for the unit sphere, then transforms the result back [S2, unofficial].

The evidence in Source [S2] explicitly describes the algorithm for computing the intersection of a ray with an ellipsoid. It details computing an inverse transformation matrix to transform the ray origin and direction into the ellipsoid's local space (accounting for scale and rotation), solving for the intersection using a quadratic equation (implied by the computation of discriminant, roots t1/t2, and the standard ray-sphere intersection logic applied to the transformed space), and then transforming the resulting intersection point back to world space. This matches the claim's description of the method.

Compute the inverse transformation matrix $M_{inv}$ that maps world space to ellipsoid local space (normalized to a unit sphere): $M_{inv} = \text{diag}(1/S_x, 1/S_y, 1/S_z) R^\top$, where $S_x, S_y, S_z$ are the components of $S$ [S2, unofficial].

The claim states that the inverse transformation matrix $M_{inv}$ is computed as $M_{inv} = diag(1/S_x, 1/S_y, 1/S_z) R^T$. The evidence from Source [S2] explicitly states: 'Compute the inverse transformation matrix: inv_transform_matrix = diag(1/S[0], 1/S[1], 1/S[2]) @ R.transpose()'. Since $S_x, S_y, S_z$ correspond to the components of $S$ (S[0], S[1], S[2]) and $R^T$ corresponds to $R.transpose()$, the evidence fully supports the claim.

Compute the forward transformation matrix $M_{fwd} = R \text{diag}(S_x, S_y, S_z)$, then $\mathbf{p} = M_{fwd} \mathbf{p}' + \mathbf{t}$ [S2, unofficial].

The claim states that the forward transformation matrix is computed as $M_{fwd} = R @ diag(S_x, S_y, S_z)$ and the point transformation is $p = M_{fwd} p' + t$. This matches the claim exactly, where $p'$ corresponds to `intersection_point_transformed` and $p$ corresponds to `intersection_point`.
